hints: Focus on the two different locations, the strong covalent bond inside one $\text{X}_2$ molecule versus the weak forces between separate $\text{X}_2$ molecules.
Notice that from chlorine to bromine to iodine the atoms get larger, so the bonded atoms are further apart and overlap less well.
Consider why physical state changes from gas ($\text{Cl}_2$) to liquid ($\text{Br}_2$) to solid ($\text{I}_2$), and what that tells you about forces between molecules.
walkthrough:
**Separate inside from between**

Think like a teacher with two pictures. Inside one molecule is a covalent bond, $\text{Cl-Cl}$, $\text{Br-Br}$, $\text{I-I}$. Between molecules are van der Waals forces, also called London dispersion forces.

**Covalent bond strength down the group**

Going down Group 17, atomic radius increases. The bonding electrons are further from the nuclei and orbital overlap is poorer, so the bond gets longer and weaker.

Trend: $\text{Cl}_2$ > $\text{Br}_2$ > $\text{I}_2$ for bond strength

**Van der Waals forces down the group**

Going down, each molecule has more electrons and a larger, more easily distorted electron cloud. That means stronger temporary dipoles and stronger London forces between molecules.

This is why boiling point increases: $\text{Cl}_2$ (gas) to $\text{Br}_2$ (liquid) to $\text{I}_2$ (solid).

**Put the two trends together**

Covalent bonds decrease in strength, while van der Waals forces increase in strength. That combination matches only one row in the table.

options.A: Half right, half wrong. Covalent bonds do decrease, but van der Waals forces do not decrease. If they decreased, boiling points would fall down the group, but they actually rise.
options.B: Correct on both. Larger atoms give longer, weaker covalent bonds inside $\text{X}_2$, while more electrons give stronger London dispersion forces between $\text{X}_2$ molecules.
options.C: Both trends reversed. Students choose this if they confuse inside and between, thinking bigger atoms make stronger covalent bonds and fewer effective attractions between molecules.
options.D: Half right, half wrong. Van der Waals forces do increase, but covalent bonds do not increase. Longer bonds with poorer overlap are weaker, not stronger.
